item.title: Still a Badass at 80s :)
item.description: womeninworldhistory At 80 years old, Nona Gaprindashvili sued Netflix for $5 million over a single line in The Queen's Gambit. The series celebrated a fictional woman conquering the male-dominated world of chess. But its finale had managed to diminish a woman who had already done exactly that. The hit drama premiered in 2020. In its final episode, set in 1968, a commentator discusses Beth Harmon's remarkable success against male opponents. He mentions the real-life women's world champion, Nona Gaprindashvili, and claims she had "never faced men." Nona knew otherwise. By 1968, she had competed against at least 59 male players, including ten grandmasters, according to her lawsuit. At a tournament in Gothenburg that year, she was the only woman in the field. She defeated seven male competitors and finished third. Born in Georgia, Nona became women's world chess champion at just 21. She defended her title repeatedly, ultimately winning five world championships and holding the crown for 16 years. In 1978, she became the first woman awarded the international grandmaster title, one of chess's highest distinctions. The television series also identified her as Russian, despite her Georgian identity. To Nona, the mistake was not a harmless detail. She had spent her career competing against men in a sport where women were routinely underestimated. In September 2021, she filed a defamation lawsuit demanding $5 million. Netflix argued that the series was fictional and that its dialogue deserved protection as creative expression. In January 2022, a federal judge rejected Netflix's attempt to have the case dismissed. A fictional work, the court explained, was not automatically immune from defamation claims involving a real person. The case ended in a confidential settlement in September 2022. No settlement amount was publicly announced. Millions had watched Beth Harmon win battles across a chessboard. Nona Gaprindashvili had been winning those battles in real tournaments decades earlier. When television rewrote that record, she challenged it in court.

item.title: 16 Years After Deepwater Horizon Spill, Deep Sea Life in The Gulf of Mexico Shows No Sign of Recovery
item.description: In 2010, the Deepwater Horizon oil rig failed catastrophically, leading to the largest oil spill in the history of Earth's oceans. About 134 million gallons of crude oil entered the Gulf of Mexico during the 87 days it took to cap the oil well, as well as 7.7 billion standard cubic feet of gas. Now, 16 years later, deep-sea ecosystems in the Gulf still show no sign of recovery from the disaster. Scientists from institutions in the US present these grim findings in a new paper published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Led by oceanographer Tracey Sutton of Nova Southeastern University, the team focused on deep pelagic marine species, which are those that live deep in the water column. They first collected net samples in 2011, right after the oil spill. When they returned in 2015 through to 2023, their samples (now more than 2,000 nets' worth, altogether) revealed a sharp crash in the abundance of deep pelagic species. "We saw this big decline," Sutton told Seth Borenstein at Associated Press. "The question was then why? So we looked at all of the natural variables we thought could account for it, namely temperature, oxygen supply, and food. None of those vary with the decline. The event that did was the oil spill. So we think that's the most likely cause of the decline." Fish numbers were down 63.5 percent; crustaceans by 62 percent; and cephalopods (mainly squid, in this context) by 59.7 percent. "The taxa that declined the most are also considered the most ecologically important in the open ocean with respect to total numbers, biogeochemical cycling, and prey provisioning for higher trophic levels," the authors write. Those taxa include krill, which declined by 72.8 percent; lanternfishes, which declined by 62.9 percent; and Cyclothone bristlemouth fishes, which declined by 69 percent. All of these animals are vital prey for the ecosystem, and fuel the fishing and tourism economies people have built around it. Many of them belong to what is known as the 'deep scattering layer', which contains fish, squid, and other creatures that rise towards the surface at night, and return to the deep at dawn, traveling hundreds of vertical meters. This daily movement is like a 'biological pump' that drives carbon sequestration in the deep ocean. "The community of organisms that comprise the deep scattering layer is a diverse complex of animals," marine scientist Kevin Boswell says. "To be able to measure changes in the ecosystem across independent methodologies really drives home the point that the midwater ecosystem has undergone a significant change." The repercussions of such a drastic collapse in the deep scattering layer may be surfacing already. Some shipboard researchers have reported sightings of 'thin whales', while once-predictable sperm whales seem to be moving erratically around the Gulf in search of food. The researchers say the oil spill is the "most parsimonious explanation" for the drastic changes to the Gulf's deep sea ecosystem. "Available evidence rules out natural phenomena as likely drivers, suggesting a large-scale pollution event and its associated mitigation measures most likely precipitated the declines," the authors write. Those associated mitigation measures include around 770,000 gallons of the chemical dispersant Corexit 9500A that were injected near the wellhead. The idea was to break up the oil and prevent massive oil slicks that could choke life on the Gulf's surface and shores, but this approach comes at a cost. The spill reached much farther than satellite images indicated, because oil residues reached all the way to the sea floor. Both the oil and the dispersant are toxic to marine life, particularly the zooplankton that form the foundation of marine food chains. Combined, they do even more damage to zooplankton than the oil does on its own. In 2014, scientists predicted that "the negative impact of crude oil and dispersant on microzooplankton may disrupt the transfer of energy from lower to higher trophic levels and change the structure and dynamics of marine planktonic communities." The new research potentially shows those outcomes in action. "Our findings are particularly concerning because these are species that are abundant, widespread, and historically might not have been considered vulnerable," says marine biologist Pedro Peres of Florida International University. https://www.sciencealert.com/16-years-after-deepwater-horizon-spill-deep-sea-life-in-the-gulf-of-mexico-shows-no-sign-of-recovery

item.title: GovBrief Today #633
item.description: The archbishop of Milwaukee publicly apologized for praying behind Donald Trump’s chair in the Oval Office. Archbishop Jeffrey Grob was one of 12 bishops invited to meet privately with Trump on Thursday. A White House aide videoed the prayer without telling them and posted it to X and Facebook that afternoon, 12 days before the midterms. Asked whether the bishops had consented, the White House responded that no president has ever been better for Catholic Americans. Des Moines Bishop William Joensen said the White House took advantage of the bishops. Grob wrote that he has since heard from people hurt by Trump’s policies, and that he went with reservations he wishes he had heeded. I’ve emailed 9,668 stories over 633 straight nights, free and without ads. The algorithm can’t show them all to you. Add your email address at govbrief.today and I will.
